newsitem.title: UK: OUTLOOK 1997-Busy year may usher in metal bull-run.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK 1997-Busy year may usher in metal bull-run.

text.p: Another lively year is likely in non-ferrous metals, and prices may be on the verge of a "bull-run" by the second half of 1997, although Chinese activity remains a major area of uncertainty, industry analysts said.
A Reuter poll of sector analysts showed the average copper price will be below 1996's $1.04/lb, but all the other metals are expected to record higher medians in 1997.

"It looks as if it will be an interesting year...Copper will once again be the key, and the Chinese are holding the balance there," analyst William Adams of London Metal Exchange (LME) trader Rudolf Wolff and Co said.
MOST MARKETS TO RECOVER FROM SUMITOMO SHOCK.

Although 1996's Sumitomo Corp scandal in copper undoubtedly poisoned sentiment throughout the base metals sector, price direction for most markets this year is not in doubt, Nick Moore of the Flemings Global Mining Group said.
"...it remains our view that with the exception of copper metal prices, particularly base metals, will be markedly stronger in 1997 and 1998," he said.
Neil Buxton of Metal Bulletin Research (MBR) noted that demand growth will gain momentum after the de-stocking which characterised 1995 and 1996.
"Rising prices, against a background of sustained economic growth should encourage some re-stocking which will add to the momentum," he added.
INVESTMENT FUND INTEREST SEEN IN SECOND HALF.
Speculators will have a part to play as well, and already the first few trading days of the year have seen investment funds nibbling in some markets.
"If oil stays strong, the funds could stay there or in bonds and not switch into the metals and other commodities for some time," Wiktor Bielski of stockbrokers Bain and Co said.
Nevertheless, analysts believe that an influx of fund interest is likely at some point this year, and this could be instrumental in a second-half rally.
"Interest rates are likely to rise in 1997 which will adversely affect equity and bond markets, which will encourage funds to diversify some of their portfolios into commodities," MBR's Buxton said.
Other factors likely to suck in fund interest are falling inventories, with the exception of copper, and relatively low price levels compared with previous bull market peaks, he added.
COPPER FINELY BALANCED, WATCHING CHINA.
In the high profile copper market - the bellwether metal on the LME - prices and stocks are delicately balanced at present.
"The Chinese are the big factor, as they effectively absorbed the forecast surplus last year," Angus MacMillan of LME trader Billiton Metals said.
China could import a similar tonnage of copper this year as it did in 1996 when it lifted some 200,000 tonnes, which would have a notable impact on the market, Bain's Bielski said.
"They (the Chinese) do need to restock their commercial inventories, and they will have to do that from imports," he said.
Stockbroker Merrill Lynch, in its annual outlook, noted that Chinese net imports could range between 250,000 and 350,000 tonnes this year.
"We then have to throw in the huge wild card of the Chinese State Reserve Bureau (SRB)," Merrill analyst Ted Arnold said.

The SRB has a mandate to import 500,000 tonnes of copper from the West under its current five-year plan, with the current stockpile some 200,000 tonnes. This implies an extra 300,000 tonnes of purchases, Merrill noted.
But if China's presence is subdued, the copper market will be vulnerable to the wave of increased supply prompted by years of artificially high prices, other analysts said.
"Whilst demand will remain robust it will be easily outpaced by supply. Between 1996 and 2000 we expect an accumulated surplus in excess of one million tonnes," Fleming's Moore said.
BUT SUPPLY GROWTH NOT INTENSE IN OTHER METALS.
The rest of the base metal metal complex will not have to contend with marked increases in production this year, which will filter through into higher prices towards the year-end.

"In 1998, capacity utilisation rates will be uncomfortably high at aluminium, nickel, and zinc producers. The market is likely to focus on these looming bottlenecks in the second half," MBR's Buxton said.
Aluminium, lead, nickel and zinc will all be in deficits this year, which will support higher prices, he added.

Aluminium in particular could benefit now that aggressive de-stocking by consumers is over and end-users decide to re-build inventories. Demand growth could be anywhere between four to six percent, analysts reckon.
"Aluminium should rise throughout the year. Nickel should do well by mid-year," analyst David Davidson at CIBC/Wood Gundy in Toronto said.
He expected zinc to move up gradually in 1997 but would not come into strength until 1998.
MARKETS WILL END YEAR EN ROUTE FOR BULL-MARKET.
By the end of 1997 all the ingredients should be in place for the another bull market, although there is unlikely to be a boom, as an oversupplied copper market will temper sentiment.
"We believe that 1997 will signal the start of a bull-market for base metals, that should peak in 1998/1999," Buxton said.
